title: Home Economics — Caring for God's Household
description: Test your understanding of cooking basics, nutrition, cleaning, laundry, basic sewing, and meal planning from a Biblical stewardship perspective.

questions.question: Which of the following is the MOST important kitchen safety rule?
options: Use the biggest knife available for every task
Always wash your hands before handling food
Cook everything on the highest heat setting
Leave the oven on when you leave the kitchen
questions.explanation: Washing your hands before handling food is a fundamental kitchen safety practice that prevents the spread of bacteria and keeps food safe to eat.

questions.question: What did Daniel choose to eat instead of the king's rich food, and what was the result?
options: He ate only bread and became weak
He ate vegetables and water, and became healthier than those who ate the king's food
He fasted completely and had miraculous strength
He ate the king's food and enjoyed it greatly
questions.explanation: Daniel chose vegetables and water over the king's rich diet. After ten days, he appeared healthier and better nourished than those who ate the royal food (Daniel 1:12-15), showing that God honors wise food choices.

questions.question: Why should you sort laundry before washing it?
options: It is not necessary — you can wash everything together
To prevent colors from bleeding onto lighter clothes and to protect delicate fabrics
To make the laundry pile look organized
Because the washing machine cannot handle mixed loads
questions.explanation: Sorting laundry prevents color bleeding (dark dyes transferring to light fabrics) and protects delicate items from damage. It is an essential step in proper clothing care.

questions.question: What is the basic stitch called where you push the needle up through fabric and back down in a line?
options: The cross stitch
The running stitch
The chain stitch
The blanket stitch
questions.explanation: The running stitch is the most basic sewing stitch. You push the needle up through the fabric, then back down a short distance away, creating small, even stitches in a straight line.

questions.question: According to John 6:12, what did Jesus tell His disciples to do after feeding the five thousand?
options: Throw away the leftover food
Give all the leftovers to the poor
Gather the leftover pieces so nothing would be wasted
Leave the leftovers for the birds
questions.explanation: Jesus instructed His disciples to gather the leftover food so nothing would be wasted. This principle of avoiding waste applies directly to meal planning and food stewardship.

questions.question: What does 'mise en place' mean in cooking?
options: Cooking at the highest temperature
Everything in its place — gathering all ingredients and tools before starting
Eating the meal as soon as it is cooked
Cleaning the kitchen after cooking
questions.explanation: 'Mise en place' is a French cooking term meaning 'everything in its place.' It means reading the recipe, gathering all ingredients and tools, and preparing them before you start cooking.

questions.question: How does meal planning help families save money?
options: It does not — meal planning costs more
By reducing food waste, avoiding impulse purchases, and cooking at home instead of eating out
By only eating one meal per day
By buying the most expensive ingredients available
questions.explanation: Meal planning saves money by helping families buy only what they need (reducing waste), stick to a grocery list (avoiding impulse buys), and cook at home (which is much cheaper than eating out).

questions.question: How did Dorcas (Tabitha) use her sewing skills to serve others?
options: She opened a clothing store for profit
She made robes and clothing for widows and those in need
She only sewed garments for the temple
She taught sewing classes at the synagogue
questions.explanation: Dorcas made robes and clothing for widows and those in need (Acts 9:39). Her sewing skills were a practical ministry that blessed her community, showing that practical skills can be used to serve God.
